sectionTitle: Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations

specStatements.text: The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
This means that chemical reactions can be represented by symbol equations which are balanced in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element involved on both sides of the equation.
Students should understand the use of the multipliers in equations in normal script before a formula and in subscript within a formula.
The relative formula mass ( M r ) of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.
In a balanced chemical equation, the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown equals the sum of the relative formula masses of the products in the quantities shown.
Students should be able to calculate the percentage by mass in a compound given the relative formula mass and the relative atomic masses.

Some reactions may appear to involve a change in mass but this can usually be explained because a reactant or product is a gas and its mass has not been taken into account. For example: when a metal reacts with oxygen the mass of the oxide produced is greater than the mass of the metal or in thermal decompositions of metal carbonates carbon dioxide is produced and escapes into the atmosphere leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.

Students should be able to explain any observed changes in mass in non-enclosed systems during a chemical reaction given the balanced symbol equation for the reaction and explain these changes in terms of the particle model.
Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained.
represent the distribution of results and make estimations of uncertainty
use the range of a set of measurements about the mean as a measure of uncertainty.

scopeNotes.statement: given the relative formula mass and the relative atomic masses
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every percentage by mass item supplies the relative formula mass of the compound and any relative atomic masses needed, exactly as the specification says students will be given them. Students are never asked to look up or derive a relative atomic mass, and the calculation is never routed through moles or masses in grams, because 4.3.1.2 asks only for a percentage worked out from relative masses.

scopeNotes.statement: explain any observed changes in mass in non-enclosed systems during a chemical reaction given the balanced symbol equation for the reaction and explain these changes in terms of the particle model
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Mass change items are set in open apparatus - an open crucible, an open test tube, an unstoppered flask - and the balanced symbol equation is printed in the stem, as the specification stipulates. Explanations are restricted to which particles enter or leave the weighed apparatus. No item requires a gas volume, a mole calculation or a rate argument, none of which belongs to 4.3.1.3.

scopeNotes.statement: this can usually be explained because a reactant or product is a gas and its mass has not been taken into account
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Apparent changes in mass are attributed only to a gaseous reactant being gained from the air or a gaseous product escaping into it. The two examples used are the two the specification names: a metal reacting with oxygen, and the thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate releasing carbon dioxide and leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product. Nothing suggests atoms are created or destroyed, and no other cause of mass change is taught.

scopeNotes.statement: use the range of a set of measurements about the mean as a measure of uncertainty.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Uncertainty is estimated only from the range of a set of repeated measurements taken about their mean, and quoted as mean plus or minus half the range. Standard deviation, percentage uncertainty and error propagation are not used anywhere, because the specification names the range about the mean as the measure required.

scopeNotes.statement: the multipliers in equations in normal script before a formula and in subscript within a formula
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Multiplier work is confined to the two positions the specification names: a number in normal script written before a formula, which multiplies every atom in that formula, and a subscript written within a formula, which multiplies only the symbol or bracketed group it follows. State symbols, oxidation numbers and charges on ions are not treated as multipliers and are not examined here.

concepts.definition: The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.

In a chemical reaction the atoms present at the start are the same atoms present at the end; they are only joined together in different ways. Because the atoms are the same atoms, the total mass cannot change.

The reactants are the substances written on the left of an equation and the products are the substances written on the right. Conservation of mass compares the total mass of all the reactants with the total mass of all the products, including any that are gases.

A symbol equation in which there is the same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the equation. Because no atoms are lost or made, every correct symbol equation for a reaction must balance in this way.

Making the numbers of atoms of each element equal on both sides by writing multipliers in normal script in front of formulae. The formulae themselves are never altered, because changing a formula changes the substance the equation describes.
A number written in normal script immediately before a formula. It multiplies every atom in that whole formula: 2Ca(OH)₂ means two of everything the formula contains, that is 2 Ca, 4 O and 4 H atoms.

A small number written below the line inside a formula. It multiplies only the symbol immediately before it: in H₂SO₄ the subscript 2 applies to hydrogen alone and the subscript 4 to oxygen alone, giving 2 H, 1 S and 4 O atoms.
A subscript written after a closing bracket multiplies everything inside the bracket. In Mg(NO₃)₂ the subscript 2 applies to the whole NO₃ group, giving 1 Mg, 2 N and 6 O atoms.
The relative mass of an atom of an element, read from the periodic table. It is a ratio, so it has no units. Relative atomic masses are the values added together to find a relative formula mass.

The relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula. For CaCO₃ this is 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100. Like Ar, it has no units.

concepts.term: Relative formula mass of a molecular element
concepts.definition: The same rule is used for an element written as a molecule. For O₂ the relative formula mass is 2 x 16 = 32, because the formula shows two oxygen atoms.

concepts.term: Conservation of relative formula mass in an equation
concepts.definition: In a balanced chemical equation, the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown equals the sum of the relative formula masses of the products in the quantities shown. The multipliers in front of the formulae must be included in both totals.

concepts.term: Percentage by mass of an element in a compound
concepts.definition: The share of a compound's relative formula mass contributed by one element: (Ar of the element x number of its atoms in the formula) divided by the Mr of the compound, then multiplied by 100. In CaCO₃ the oxygen is (3 x 16) / 100 x 100 = 48%.

A change in the reading on a balance during a reaction. Some reactions may appear to involve a change in mass, but this can usually be explained because a reactant or product is a gas and its mass has not been taken into account.

concepts.term: Mass increase when a metal reacts with oxygen
concepts.definition: When a metal reacts with oxygen the mass of the oxide produced is greater than the mass of the metal, because oxygen atoms from the air have been added to the solid being weighed.

concepts.term: Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate
concepts.definition: Heating a metal carbonate breaks it down: carbon dioxide is produced and escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product. The mass of solid left is therefore less than the mass of carbonate heated.

Apparatus that is open to the air, so gases can enter it or leave it during a reaction. Mass is still conserved overall; it is only the mass sitting on the balance that changes, because some of the substance has moved into or out of the apparatus.
Apparatus sealed so that no particles can enter or leave, such as a stoppered flask. Any gas made stays inside and is still weighed, so the balance reading does not change during the reaction.

concepts.term: Particle model explanation of a mass change
concepts.definition: Explaining a balance reading by saying which particles have crossed the boundary of the apparatus. Gas particles are spread far apart and are invisible, but they still have mass, so particles leaving lower the reading and particles joining from the air raise it.

Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained. Uncertainty is a statement of the interval within which the true value is expected to lie; it is not the same thing as a mistake.

The pattern formed by a set of repeated measurements when they are set out, for example in a table, a scatter of points on a number line or a bar chart. Displaying the distribution shows how closely the repeats agree and makes any odd value obvious.
The sum of a set of repeated measurements divided by how many there are. The mean is the value the uncertainty is quoted about, and it is calculated after any anomalous result has been left out.
A measurement that lies well outside the distribution formed by the others. It is identified and excluded before the mean and the range are worked out, otherwise it would distort both.
The difference between the largest and the smallest value in a set of measurements. For 24.10, 24.15 and 24.20 cm³ the range is 24.20 - 24.10 = 0.10 cm³.

The range of a set of measurements about the mean is used as a measure of uncertainty: the result is quoted as the mean plus or minus half the range. A mean of 24.15 cm³ with a range of 0.10 cm³ is written 24.15 ± 0.05 cm³. A wider range means a larger uncertainty.

misconceptions.question: A beaker of acid and marble chips loses 0.8 g while it fizzes. Has mass been destroyed?
misconceptions.correct: No. The 0.8 g has left the beaker as carbon dioxide gas. Collect the gas and the total mass is unchanged, because no atoms are lost or made.
misconceptions.misconception: When a gas bubbles away, that mass is gone - it has been used up by the reaction, so mass really is lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students trust the balance over the law. A gas is invisible and disperses, so it stops feeling like a substance at all, and the falling reading looks like direct evidence that matter has disappeared.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the atoms went, not where the mass went. Every carbon and oxygen atom in the escaping gas came from the marble and the acid and still exists; the balance simply no longer has them on it.

misconceptions.question: Burning magnesium leaves a solid heavier than the metal. Have extra atoms been made?
misconceptions.correct: No atoms are made. Oxygen atoms from the air have joined the magnesium, so the oxide contains the mass of both the metal and the oxygen that reacted.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction creates new material, which is why the product weighs more than what you started with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is often taught with the mass loss case only. When a reading rises instead, students reach for the opposite explanation and assume matter has been generated, since nothing visible was added.
misconceptions.correction: Point at the air. The reactant that raised the mass was already there as an invisible gas; weigh the crucible with a lid on and the gain still comes from oxygen entering, never from new atoms.

misconceptions.question: To balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, may the water be rewritten as H₂O₂?
misconceptions.correct: No. Balance by writing multipliers in front of formulae: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. The formula H₂O must not be altered.
misconceptions.misconception: You can balance an equation by changing the little subscript numbers until the atoms come out equal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is met as an arithmetic puzzle, and the subscripts are the numbers most easily adjusted to make the sums work. The chemical meaning of a formula gets lost behind the counting.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what H₂O₂ is. It is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance with different properties. Changing a subscript changes the chemical, so the equation is no longer about the reaction being described.

misconceptions.question: Is Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂ balanced, since every substance appears once on each side?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are 2 H atoms on the left and 3 on the right. The balanced equation is 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
misconceptions.misconception: An equation is balanced when the same symbols appear on both sides, or when there are as many formulae on the left as on the right.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students match what they can see quickly. Comparing whole formulae is far easier than counting atoms element by element, and it gives the right answer often enough to feel reliable.
misconceptions.correction: Insist on an atom tally for each element, written out under the equation. Balancing is defined in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element on both sides, not the numbers of formulae.

misconceptions.question: A student balances the sodium in 2Na + H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ and stops. Is the equation finished?
misconceptions.correct: No. Oxygen and hydrogen are still unequal. Every element has to balance at the same time, which needs 2H₂O on the left.
misconceptions.misconception: Once the metal, or whichever element you dealt with first, has the same number on each side, the equation is balanced.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first element balanced is usually the easiest one, and the sense of having solved something makes students stop checking. Nothing on the page signals that the other elements have shifted.
misconceptions.correction: Re-count every element after each change. Adding a multiplier to fix one element almost always disturbs another, so balancing is finished only when a full tally shows all elements equal.

misconceptions.question: How many atoms of each element are shown by 2MgCl₂?
misconceptions.correct: 2 Mg and 4 Cl. The 2 in normal script multiplies everything in the formula, including the chlorine that already carries a subscript 2.
misconceptions.misconception: The big number in front only applies to the first element written in the formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The multiplier sits directly against the first symbol, so it reads as belonging to that symbol alone, the way an adjective attaches to the nearest noun.
misconceptions.correction: Read the multiplier as 'two lots of the whole formula'. Write the formula out twice if necessary: MgCl₂ MgCl₂ makes 2 Mg and 4 Cl unmistakable.

misconceptions.question: How many hydrogen atoms are shown by 2H₂O?
misconceptions.correct: 4. The 2 in front and the subscript 2 are multiplied together, giving 2 x 2 = 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: The number in front is just a label saying how many molecules there are, so you count either it or the subscript, not both.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two numbers of different kinds sit in one expression and students treat them as alternatives rather than factors. Only one number is usually needed in the simpler examples met first.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two jobs, then combine them. The subscript says how many atoms are in one molecule; the multiplier says how many molecules there are; the atom count is the product of the two.

misconceptions.question: How many oxygen atoms are shown by Mg(NO₃)₂?
misconceptions.correct: 6. The subscript 2 after the bracket multiplies the whole NO₃ group, so there are 2 N atoms and 6 O atoms as well as 1 Mg.
misconceptions.misconception: The number after the bracket belongs to the atom just before it, so only the oxygen, or only the last symbol, gets doubled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other subscript students meet does apply to the single symbol on its left, so the rule is generalised straight past the bracket without noticing that the bracket has changed what it is attached to.
misconceptions.correction: Treat the bracket as one parcel. Whatever is inside it is repeated as many times as the subscript says, so Mg(NO₃)₂ is Mg with two complete NO₃ groups.

misconceptions.question: The Mr of CO₂ is 44. Is that 44 grams?
misconceptions.correct: No. Relative formula mass is a ratio of masses, so it has no units. It is written simply as 44.
misconceptions.misconception: Relative formula mass is a mass, so it must be measured in grams like everything else you weigh.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word mass is in the name, and in later work the same number does appear in gram quantities. Students see a number that behaves like a mass and supply the familiar unit.
misconceptions.correction: Stress the word relative. Mr compares the mass of one formula unit with the relative atomic masses used to build it; a comparison has no unit, so no gram symbol is written.

misconceptions.question: What is the relative formula mass of CaCO₃? (Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16)
misconceptions.correct: 100. The three oxygen atoms shown by the subscript each contribute 16, so Mr = 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100.
misconceptions.misconception: You add up the relative atomic mass of each element in the formula once, so CaCO₃ gives 40 + 12 + 16 = 68.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the formula as a list of ingredients rather than as a count of atoms, and the subscript is small and easily skipped when the periodic table values are being copied out.
misconceptions.correction: Write the atom count beside each symbol before adding anything. Mr is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula, so each subscript must multiply its own Ar.

misconceptions.question: A student calculates the Mr of CaCO₃ as 40 + 12 + 16 + 3 = 71. Where is the error?
misconceptions.correct: The subscript 3 must multiply the Ar of oxygen, not be added to the total: 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100.
misconceptions.misconception: Every number in the formula gets added into the total, so the subscript is another number to include in the sum.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The calculation is remembered as 'add up the numbers in the formula'. Once addition is the only operation in mind, any digit on the page is treated as another term.
misconceptions.correction: Say what each number counts. The subscript counts atoms and the Ar gives the mass of one of them, so they multiply; only the totals for different elements are added.

misconceptions.question: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how are the relative formula masses compared on the two sides?
misconceptions.correct: Include the multipliers: (2 x 2) + 32 = 36 on the left and 2 x 18 = 36 on the right. The totals are equal.
misconceptions.misconception: You compare the Mr of one formula on the left with the Mr of one formula on the right, so 2 and 32 against 18 shows they do not match.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative formula mass is learned for single compounds first, so the habit is to work out one formula at a time and the equation's multipliers are treated as decoration.
misconceptions.correction: Read the specification wording literally: the sum of the relative formula masses in the quantities shown. Each multiplier is part of the quantity, so multiply each Mr by the number in front of it before adding.

misconceptions.question: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, does 2 g of magnesium react with 32 g of oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: No. The numbers in an equation count formulae and the Mr values are relative masses, not masses in grams. The equation gives ratios, not weighings.
misconceptions.misconception: The balancing numbers and the Mr values tell you directly how many grams of each substance you need.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The totals on each side really do behave like masses, and questions often go on to use grams, so students collapse the distinction between a relative mass and a measured mass.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two apart. The equation fixes the ratio in which relative masses combine; grams only appear once an actual quantity is stated in the question.

misconceptions.question: Why do the relative formula mass totals on the two sides of a balanced equation agree?
misconceptions.correct: Because the same atoms appear on both sides, only rearranged. The multipliers are chosen to balance atoms, and equal mass totals follow from that.
misconceptions.misconception: The numbers in front of the formulae are picked so that the two mass totals come out the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the totals match every time and infer that matching them was the goal, reversing cause and effect in a rule that always seems to work.
misconceptions.correction: Balance an equation without ever mentioning mass, then add the Mr totals afterwards. They agree because the atom counts agree, which is conservation of mass showing itself, not a target that was aimed at.

misconceptions.question: What percentage by mass of CaCO₃ (Mr 100) is oxygen? (Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16)
misconceptions.correct: 48%. The oxygen contributes 3 x 16 = 48 out of a relative formula mass of 100.
misconceptions.misconception: Three of the five atoms are oxygen, so the answer is 60%.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Percentage is met first as a share of a count, and counting atoms in a formula is quicker than working with relative atomic masses. The method feels right because it does produce a sensible-looking percentage.
misconceptions.correction: Ask which is heavier, an oxygen atom or a calcium atom. Since atoms differ in mass, a share of the atoms is not a share of the mass; only masses may be divided by masses.

misconceptions.question: What percentage by mass of H₂SO₄ (Mr 98) is hydrogen? (Ar: H 1)
misconceptions.correct: About 2.0%. There are two hydrogen atoms, so the calculation is (2 x 1) / 98 x 100.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen has an Ar of 1, so you use 1 over 98 whatever the formula says.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The relative atomic mass is copied straight from the periodic table, and the subscript is treated as part of the formula's name rather than as a count that belongs in the calculation.
misconceptions.correction: Build the numerator in two steps, always: the Ar of the element multiplied by how many of its atoms the formula shows. The denominator is the Mr, which already contains both of them.

misconceptions.question: Magnesium is heated in an open crucible until it has all reacted. Does the solid lose mass?
misconceptions.correct: No, it gains mass. When a metal reacts with oxygen the mass of the oxide produced is greater than the mass of the metal.
misconceptions.misconception: Burning destroys things, so the magnesium burns away and less is left behind than you started with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday burning - wood, paper, a candle - leaves a small pile of ash, so students generalise that combustion always removes material rather than adding a reactant from the air.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the two cases. Wood loses mass because its gaseous products drift off; magnesium keeps its product as a solid and gains the oxygen as well, so the crucible ends heavier.

misconceptions.question: Copper carbonate is heated: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. Why does the solid lose mass?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide is produced and escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the copper oxide as the only solid product.
misconceptions.misconception: The heat destroys part of the carbonate, or the solid evaporates away as copper carbonate vapour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heating is associated with evaporation and with things being burnt up. Without the equation in front of them, students explain the loss with a physical change instead of naming the gas produced.
misconceptions.correction: Read the products off the equation. One product is a gas and the other is a solid; the gas leaves the tube and takes its mass with it, and no atoms are destroyed at any point.

misconceptions.question: A solid is heated and its mass reading rises. Is this because heating makes it expand?
misconceptions.correct: No. Expansion changes volume, not mass. A rise in the reading means matter has been added, such as oxygen from the air combining with the solid.
misconceptions.misconception: Hot things expand and get bigger, and bigger means heavier, so heating on its own changes the mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Size and mass are bound together in everyday thinking, and expansion is the effect of heating that students recall most readily, so it is offered whenever heat and a mass change appear together.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two ideas with a test: heat a solid that does not react and the balance does not move. Only a chemical change that adds or removes particles alters the mass.

misconceptions.question: Mass falls during a reaction in an open flask. Does that break the law of conservation of mass?
misconceptions.correct: No. The law holds everywhere. In a non-enclosed system a gaseous product has left the flask, so the balance is no longer weighing all of the products.
misconceptions.misconception: Conservation of mass is a rule about sealed containers; in an open beaker mass genuinely can be lost or gained.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every demonstration that shows constant mass uses a stoppered flask, so the seal is remembered as a condition for the law rather than as a way of keeping the products where they can be weighed.
misconceptions.correction: Name the system. Mass is conserved for the reaction as a whole; the seal only decides whether all the products stay on the balance. Weigh the escaping gas too and the total is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Does the carbon dioxide leaving a flask actually weigh anything?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Gas particles have mass, so 22 g of carbon dioxide leaving the flask lowers the reading by 22 g.
misconceptions.misconception: Gases are weightless - they float away, so a gas cannot make any difference to a balance reading.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gases cannot be seen or felt, and they rise out of the apparatus, which looks like the behaviour of something with no weight. Nothing in everyday experience makes the mass of air obvious.
misconceptions.correction: Point to the numbers. The mass that disappeared from the balance is exactly the mass of gas made, which is only possible if the gas particles carry that mass with them.

misconceptions.question: A gas is produced inside a sealed flask on a balance. Does the reading rise?
misconceptions.correct: No, it stays the same. The same particles are present, all still inside the flask, so the total mass on the balance is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: The gas particles push outwards on the sealed flask as they move, and that pressure adds to the reading.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know a gas exerts pressure and know a balance measures a downward force, so the two are merged. The particles pressing on the walls feels as though it should register as extra weight.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what has entered or left. Nothing has, so nothing on the balance has changed. Pressure acts in all directions inside the flask and does not add mass to it.

misconceptions.question: Five repeats of the same measurement give five slightly different values. Can that be avoided?
misconceptions.correct: No. Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained, so repeats will not agree exactly however carefully they are taken.
misconceptions.misconception: If you work carefully enough, or use good enough apparatus, you can measure the true value exactly and every repeat will match.
misconceptions.whyItArises: School practicals are marked for care and neatness, so disagreement between repeats is read as a personal failing rather than as a property of measurement itself.
misconceptions.correction: Show that even the best equipment has a smallest division and a reading judgement. Uncertainty can be reduced and estimated, but it is never removed, which is why results are quoted with a range.

misconceptions.question: Is an uncertainty of ± 0.05 cm³ an admission that a mistake was made?
misconceptions.correct: No. It states the interval in which the true value is expected to lie. A mistake is an error in what was done and would be corrected, not quoted.
misconceptions.misconception: Uncertainty means you got it wrong, so quoting one is owning up to sloppy work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In ordinary English 'uncertain' means unsure or unreliable, and the word 'error' is used loosely in class for both mistakes and measurement uncertainty, so the two collapse together.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish them by what you would do next. A mistake is put right and the measurement repeated; an uncertainty is estimated from the spread of good repeats and reported with the result.

misconceptions.question: Four titres agree to within 0.1 cm³ and a fifth is 1.7 cm³ higher. Should all five be averaged?
misconceptions.correct: No. Setting the results out shows the fifth lies well outside the distribution, so it is anomalous and is left out of the mean and the range.
misconceptions.misconception: All the results must go into the mean, because leaving one out would be changing the data to suit yourself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are told not to fiddle with results, and excluding a value looks like exactly that. The difference between discarding an identified anomaly and discarding an inconvenient value is not obvious.
misconceptions.correction: Make the decision visible and justified. Display the distribution, state which value sits apart from it and why it is treated as anomalous, then calculate the mean from the rest.

misconceptions.question: For 24.10, 24.15 and 24.20 cm³, what is the range?
misconceptions.correct: 0.10 cm³. The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values: 24.20 - 24.10.
misconceptions.misconception: The range is the biggest value in the set, so the range is 24.20 cm³.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech a range is the span a thing covers, and the largest number is the most striking one on the page. Students report a value from the data instead of a difference between two of them.
misconceptions.correction: Make it a subtraction every time. The range measures how spread out the results are, so it must be small when they agree closely - 24.20 cm³ would say the readings differ by a whole 24 cm³.

misconceptions.question: The mean is 24.15 cm³ and the range is 0.10 cm³. How is the result quoted?
misconceptions.correct: 24.15 ± 0.05 cm³. The range is used about the mean, so half of it goes on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: You write the mean plus or minus the whole range, giving 24.15 ± 0.10 cm³.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The range is the number just calculated, so it is the number that gets written down. That the plus-or-minus sign covers an interval of twice that width is easy to overlook.
misconceptions.correction: Draw the interval on a number line. The results run from the smallest to the largest, and the mean sits between them, so the distance from the mean to each end is half the range.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is the law of conservation of mass?

options.text: Atoms are destroyed when a gas escapes, so the mass of the products falls.
options.rationale: Students who trust a falling balance reading over the law conclude that the escaping gas has been destroyed.

options.text: The masses are equal only when the reaction happens in a sealed container.
options.rationale: Every classroom demonstration of constant mass uses a stopper, so the seal is remembered as a condition of the law.

options.text: The number of molecules is unchanged, so the total mass cannot change.
options.rationale: Picked by students who track whole formulae rather than atoms; molecule numbers often do change, as in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

options.text: No atoms are lost or made, so the products have the same mass as the reactants.
options.rationale: This is the law as the specification states it: the atoms are conserved, and the equality of masses follows from that.

mcqs.stem: 4.8 g of magnesium is heated in air and reacts completely with 3.2 g of oxygen. What is the mass of magnesium oxide formed?

options.rationale: All the atoms in both reactants end up in the oxide, so its mass is 4.8 + 3.2 = 8.0 g.
Chosen by students who treat the oxygen as weightless, so only the magnesium is thought to contribute mass.
Comes from subtracting, on the assumption that reacting must use mass up rather than combine it.
The mass of the oxygen alone, selected by students who take the last number in the stem as the answer.

mcqs.stem: Which equation for the reaction of sodium with water is correctly balanced?

options.text: Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂
options.rationale: Looks balanced to students who check that each substance appears once on each side; in fact there are 2 H left and 3 H right.

options.text: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
options.rationale: Both sides show 2 Na, 4 H and 2 O atoms, so every element balances.

options.text: 2Na + H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
options.rationale: The sodium has been balanced and the work stopped there, leaving hydrogen and oxygen unequal.

options.text: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + 2H₂
options.rationale: Doubling everything in sight over-supplies hydrogen: 4 H on the left against 6 H on the right.

mcqs.stem: A student tries to balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by rewriting the product as H₂O₂. Why is this not acceptable?

options.text: It is allowed as long as the same subscript change is made on the other side.
options.rationale: Students who treat subscripts as adjustable numbers look for a rule that makes the change legitimate.

options.text: The atoms now balance, but the equation shows too many molecules.
options.rationale: Chosen by students counting formulae rather than atoms, who see nothing wrong with the atom tally itself.

options.text: H₂O₂ is a different substance, so the equation no longer shows this reaction.
options.rationale: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide. Changing a subscript changes the chemical, so balancing must be done with multipliers in front instead.

options.text: Hydrogen and oxygen cannot form a compound with two oxygen atoms.
options.rationale: Sounds like a chemical objection, but hydrogen peroxide exists; the problem is that it is not the product of this reaction.

mcqs.stem: How many atoms in total are shown by 2Ca(OH)₂?

options.rationale: Obtained by applying the multiplier 2 to each symbol once and ignoring the bracket, giving 2 Ca, 2 O and 2 H.
Comes from applying the bracket subscript only to the hydrogen, giving 1 Ca, 1 O and 2 H before doubling.
Each Ca(OH)₂ has 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H, which is 5 atoms; the multiplier 2 doubles all of them.
The count for a single formula unit, with the number in front read as a label rather than a multiplier.

mcqs.stem: In the equation 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what does the 2 written in front of MgO tell you?

options.text: Two extra oxygen atoms are joined to each magnesium oxide.
options.rationale: Confuses the multiplier with a subscript, which is what would alter the atoms inside one formula.

options.text: Twice as much magnesium oxide forms, by mass, as magnesium.
options.rationale: Reads the balancing number as a mass ratio; it counts formulae, and here the mass ratio is not 2 anyway.

options.text: Two units of magnesium oxide: two Mg atoms and two O atoms.
options.rationale: A multiplier in normal script multiplies every atom in the formula that follows it.

options.text: The magnesium is doubled, but the oxygen in it is not.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who attach the multiplier to the first symbol it touches rather than to the whole formula.

mcqs.stem: What is the relative formula mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16)

options.rationale: Each element counted once, 40 + 12 + 16, with the subscript 3 overlooked.
The subscript has been added to the total instead of multiplying the oxygen: 40 + 12 + 16 + 3.
Two oxygens counted instead of three, a slip made when the formula is copied out from memory.
40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100, using each relative atomic mass in the number shown in the formula.

mcqs.stem: What is the relative formula mass of magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO₃)₂? (Ar: Mg 24, N 14, O 16)

options.rationale: The subscript 2 multiplies the whole NO₃ group: 24 + 2 x (14 + 48) = 148.
The bracket subscript has been applied to the oxygen only, giving 6 O but leaving a single nitrogen.
The bracket subscript is ignored altogether, so only one NO₃ group is counted: 24 + 14 + 48.
The 2 outside the bracket is added to the total rather than used to multiply the group.

mcqs.stem: 50 g of calcium carbonate is heated in an open tube until it fully decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The calcium oxide left has a mass of 28 g. What mass of carbon dioxide escaped?

options.rationale: The relative formula mass of CO₂ quoted as though it were the mass in grams produced in this experiment.
The masses of the products must total the 50 g of reactant, so the gas accounts for 50 - 28 = 22 g.

options.text: 0 g
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe gases weigh nothing, so the escaping carbon dioxide is thought to carry no mass.
The two given masses added, which would mean the products weigh more in total than the carbonate heated.

mcqs.stem: In a balanced equation, why does the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants equal that of the products?

options.text: Every reaction is done in a sealed container, so nothing at all can escape.
options.rationale: Applies the sealed-flask demonstration to the equation itself, which holds whatever apparatus is used.

options.text: The same atoms are present on both sides, just rearranged, so the totals match.
options.rationale: Equal atom counts of every element mean the same relative atomic masses are being added up on each side.

options.text: The balancing numbers are chosen to make the two mass totals come out equal.
options.rationale: Reverses cause and effect: the multipliers are chosen to balance atoms, and the mass totals then agree.

options.text: Each formula on the left has the same relative formula mass as one on the right.
options.rationale: Compares formulae one at a time; the specification requires the sums in the quantities shown.

mcqs.stem: Calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, has a relative formula mass of 100. What is the percentage by mass of oxygen in it? (Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16)

options.rationale: Three oxygen atoms contribute 3 x 16 = 48 out of the relative formula mass of 100.
Three of the five atoms are oxygen, so students who take a share of the atoms rather than of the mass get 60%.
The relative atomic mass of one oxygen atom used, with the subscript 3 left out of the numerator.
Two oxygen atoms counted instead of three, an arithmetic slip in an otherwise correct method.

mcqs.stem: Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, has a relative formula mass of 80. What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in it? (Ar: N 14, H 1, O 16)

options.rationale: Only one nitrogen atom used in the numerator, giving 14 / 80 x 100.
Two of the nine atoms in the formula are nitrogen, which gives 22.2% if atoms are counted instead of masses.
The formula shows two nitrogen atoms, so (2 x 14) / 80 x 100 = 35.0%.
The percentage by mass of oxygen, 48 / 80 x 100, calculated for the wrong element in the compound.

mcqs.stem: Sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, has a relative formula mass of 98. Which expression gives the percentage by mass of hydrogen in it? (Ar: H 1)

options.rationale: The relative atomic mass of hydrogen used as it stands, without multiplying by the two atoms in the formula.
The formula shows two hydrogen atoms, each of relative atomic mass 1, out of a relative formula mass of 98.
Two of the seven atoms are hydrogen, so this is the share of the atoms rather than the share of the mass.
The fraction is inverted, which gives a percentage far above 100 and so cannot be a share of the compound.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium ribbon is heated in an open crucible until it has fully reacted. What happens to the mass of the solid, and why?

options.text: It rises, because oxygen from the air has combined with the magnesium.
options.rationale: When a metal reacts with oxygen the mass of the oxide produced is greater than the mass of the metal.

options.text: It falls, because the magnesium burns away and is lost into the air.
options.rationale: Everyday burning leaves less behind, so students expect combustion always to remove material.

options.text: It rises, because heating expands the metal and larger pieces weigh more.
options.rationale: Gets the direction right for the wrong reason, treating expansion as a gain in mass rather than in volume.

options.text: It stays the same, since no atoms can be gained or lost from the crucible.
options.rationale: Assumes an invisible gas cannot add mass, so conservation is applied to the solid alone.

mcqs.stem: Copper carbonate is heated in an open test tube: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. The mass of solid in the tube falls. Why?

options.text: Heat from the flame has destroyed some of the carbon and oxygen atoms.
options.rationale: Explains the loss by destroying atoms, which conservation of mass rules out in any reaction.

options.text: The solid evaporates, so copper carbonate is lost from the tube as vapour.
options.rationale: Substitutes a physical change for the decomposition the equation in the stem actually shows.

options.text: The copper oxide formed is less dense than the copper carbonate was.
options.rationale: Confuses a property that depends on volume with the quantity a balance measures.

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas is produced and escapes, taking its mass away.
options.rationale: The carbon dioxide leaves the tube, so the copper oxide is the only solid product left to be weighed.

mcqs.stem: In an open flask on a balance, calcium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The reading falls. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Mass is not conserved here, because the flask was not sealed with a bung.
options.rationale: Treats the seal as a condition for the law rather than as a way of keeping the products on the balance.

options.text: The carbon dioxide produced has no mass of its own, so the products weigh less.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think gases are weightless; the fall is exactly the mass of the gas that left.

options.text: Some of the acid particles have been destroyed in making the new products.
options.rationale: The acid is used up, but its atoms are all still present in the calcium chloride and the water formed.

options.text: Mass is conserved; the carbon dioxide has left and is no longer weighed.
options.rationale: The equation shows a gaseous product. In a non-enclosed system it escapes, so the balance no longer holds all the products.

mcqs.stem: The same reaction is repeated in a flask sealed with a bung, standing on a balance. What happens to the reading?

options.text: It stays the same, because the carbon dioxide is still inside the flask.
options.rationale: No particles enter or leave, so every atom that was weighed at the start is still being weighed at the end.

options.text: It falls, because once the carbon is a gas its particles have no mass.
options.rationale: Gas particles have mass whether they are free to leave or not, so being sealed in changes nothing.

options.text: It rises, because the gas particles press outwards on the sealed flask.
options.rationale: Merges pressure with weight; the particles push in all directions and add no mass to the flask.

options.text: It falls a little, because gas can pass out through the glass walls.
options.rationale: Plausible to students who picture gases as able to seep anywhere, but a sealed flask holds them in.

mcqs.stem: 0.24 g of magnesium ribbon is burned in an open crucible and 0.40 g of white solid is left. Which statement explains the increase in terms of the particle model?

options.text: The magnesium particles have grown larger as they took in heat energy.
options.rationale: Uses expansion, which changes how much space particles occupy, not how much mass they have.

options.text: Oxygen molecules from the air have bonded to magnesium in the solid.
options.rationale: Particles have crossed into the crucible from the air, so the solid now contains 0.16 g of oxygen as well as the metal.

options.text: Extra particles were created in the crucible as the bright flame burned.
options.rationale: Students who see a rise in mass without anything visible being added assume matter was made.

options.text: Air became trapped between the particles of the white powder as it formed.
options.rationale: A tempting picture because the product is powdery, but trapped air would not be held there on the balance.

mcqs.stem: A student measures the same volume of solution five times and gets five slightly different readings. What does this show?

options.text: The student was careless; accurate work gives the same value each time.
options.rationale: Practical work is marked for care, so students read disagreement between repeats as a personal failing.

options.text: Whenever a measurement is made there is some uncertainty in the result.
options.rationale: Uncertainty is a property of measurement itself, so repeated readings are not expected to agree exactly.

options.text: A mistake has been made, so all five of the readings must be wrong.
options.rationale: Treats uncertainty as the same thing as an error in what was done, which would be corrected rather than quoted.

options.text: The volume of the solution changed a little between the readings.
options.rationale: Invents a change in the thing measured, when it is the measuring that varies from repeat to repeat.

mcqs.stem: A student records five titres: 24.10, 24.15, 24.20, 25.90 and 24.15 cm³. What should be done before estimating the uncertainty?

options.text: Include all five of the titres in the mean, since every reading must be used.
options.rationale: Students told not to alter data see excluding an identified anomaly as the same as discarding an awkward result.

options.text: Use 25.90 as the measure of spread, as it is the largest value found.
options.rationale: Reports a value from the data instead of the difference between the largest and smallest values.

options.text: Repeat the titration once more and report only that final reading.
options.rationale: Discards the evidence of spread entirely, leaving no way to estimate the uncertainty at all.

options.text: Set the results out to show their distribution and treat 25.90 as anomalous.
options.rationale: Displaying the distribution makes the value lying outside it obvious, and it is excluded before the mean and range are found.

mcqs.stem: Four titres are recorded: 24.10, 24.15, 24.20 and 24.15 cm³. What is the range of these measurements?

options.rationale: The largest measurement reported as the range, rather than the difference between two of them.

options.text: 0.05 cm³
options.rationale: Half the range, which is the uncertainty quoted either side of the mean, not the range itself.

options.text: 0.10 cm³
options.rationale: The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values: 24.20 - 24.10 = 0.10 cm³.
The mean of the four titres, given by students who confuse the average with the spread.

mcqs.stem: The mean of a set of titres is 24.15 cm³ and their range is 0.10 cm³. How should the result be quoted?

options.rationale: The range is used about the mean, so half of it is placed on each side of the mean value.
The whole range written after the plus-or-minus sign, which describes an interval twice as wide as the results.
The largest titre used in place of the mean, so the interval is centred on the wrong value.
The range doubled rather than halved, which overstates how far the results actually spread.
